extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy and natural science; philosophers and theorists interested in general theory of Evolution and Dissolution
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for what counts as a satisfactory philosophical system (a unified theory of change), focusing on laws like the Persistence of Force and the continuous redistribution of Matter and Motion; used to evaluate philosophical/theoretical accounts of evolution/dissolution across scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy as completely unified knowledge
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats the highest form of Philosophy as an integrated, unified body of knowledge; successful philosophical systems ought to achieve this unification by showing how their component truths fit together rather than remaining disconnected. (See §185: 'Philosophy — when we compared men's various conceptions...we found in them all, the tacit implication that Philosophy is completely unified knowledge.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental propositions must be established by congruity of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental propositions, or propositions not deducible from deeper ones, can be established only by showing the complete congruity of all the results reached through the assumption of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundational premises should be assumed provisionally and then validated by demonstrating that all consequences derived from them cohere; in other words, show that assuming a fundamental proposition yields results fully congruous with experience and other truths (used as the method for choosing data for Philosophy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of Force as the ultimate ground-truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The Persistence of Force is ultimate; other primary truths (Indestructibility of Matter, Continuity of Motion) are derivative from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that Force being unchangeable in quantity is the deepest truth from which indestructibility of Matter and continuity of Motion follow. A philosophical system should identify such an ultimate principle and derive other primary truths from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of the relations among forces (Uniformity of Law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Persistence of the Relations among Forces (ordinarily called Uniformity of Law) follows from the fact that Force can neither arise out of nothing nor lapse into nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adequate theory must account for the uniformity of natural law as an implication of conservation: relations among forces persist because forces are neither created nor destroyed. This is treated as a necessary implication rather than an independent assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation/correlation of forces (transformation, not loss)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forces which seem to be lost are transformed into their equivalents of other forces; conversely, forces which become manifest do so by disappearance of pre-existing equivalent forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses this as an explanatory criterion across domains (motions of heavenly bodies, terrestrial changes, organic and super-organic actions). A satisfactory account should trace apparent losses/gains of force to transformations into equivalent forms rather than positing creation or annihilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of least resistance (direction of motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything moves along the line of least resistance, or the line of greatest traction, or their resultant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is claimed to hold at all scales—from stellar motions to nervous discharges and economic currents—and is shown to follow from Persistence of Force. A good theory should explain phenomena as motions proceeding along these resultant lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm of Motion (inevitable alternation)
rubrics_metrics.description: All motion alternates; perpetual reversal of Motion between limits (rhythm) is inevitable given the persistence of force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adequate philosophical account must predict or explain alternating/cyclic behavior (e.g., orbital motions, molecular undulations, cadences of speech, rises/falls of prices) as necessary consequences of persistent forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of co-operation of all factors (continuous re-distribution of Matter and Motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy must formulate the law of the co-operation of all the factors — a law expressing simultaneously the complex antecedents and consequents which any phenomenon presents; concretely, the universal law is the continuous re-distribution of Matter and Motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond listing elemental laws, a satisfactory philosophy must give a single formula/law that unifies how all factors combine. The author identifies this universal law as the continuous redistribution of matter and motion, which should apply to every change and unify all phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness over whole history (imperceptible ↔ perceptible)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Philosophy is inadequate if it does not formulate the whole series of changes passed through by every existence in its passage from the imperceptible to the perceptible and from the perceptible to the imperceptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The required law must apply to full temporal histories of entities (their origins and destinies), not just to their present concrete forms. The system must account for both antecedent and subsequent phases of any phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula must define concentration and diffusion in terms of Matter and Motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The universal formula sought must define the opposite processes of concentration and diffusion in terms of Matter and Motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentration (integration of matter) and diffusion (disintegration) are to be expressed as reciprocal relationships involving redistribution of motion and matter: concentration of matter implies dissipation of motion, and absorption of motion implies diffusion of matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Evolution and Dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution = integration of Matter and dissipation of Motion; Dissolution (the complementary process) is the diffusion or disintegration resulting when motion is added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissolution is treated as sufficiently defined by these terms; Evolution often requires a more detailed account because it commonly involves secondary redistributions. A theory should distinguish and define both processes and show how they alternate in cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs. Compound Evolution (secondary redistributions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution distinguishes into simple and compound: simple evolution is primary redistribution (integration + dissipation of motion), whereas compound evolution includes secondary redistributions (formation of parts, increased heterogeneity and definiteness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether secondary redistributions occur depends on conditions that hinder the dissipation of motion (e.g., the largeness of the aggregate or peculiar constitution of components). A satisfactory account must explain when and why evolution produces mere integration or additional structural/functional differentiation, and give examples across inorganic, organic, and super-organic domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural complexity parallels functional complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Every increase in structural complexity involves a corresponding increase in functional complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text asserts this as a general pattern—from integration of molecules into masses to formation of organs in organisms and division of labor in societies. Evaluations should check that a proposed theory accounts for the emergent functional changes accompanying structural differentiation.
